newsitem.title: USA: U.S. "disappointed" with Israeli delay on funds.
newsitem.headline: U.S. "disappointed" with Israeli delay on funds.

text.p: The United States said on Friday it was disappointed at Israel's delay in releasing funds to the Palestinian Authority but expected the dispute to go away within a matter of days.

Israel withheld the tax money and customs duties after two Palestinian suicide bombers killed 16 people at a Jerusalem market on July 30. Palestinian leaders say it is a form of collective punishment.

Danny Naveh, senior adviser to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, told Israel Radio on Friday that the disagreement came up during this week's visit to the region by U.S. Middle East envoy Dennis Ross.

U.S. State Department spokesman James Rubin, asked if Ross felt the Israelis had reneged on a promise to release the money, restated the U.S. position that withholding the funds and tight Israeli restrictions on the movement of Palestinians were "unwise" and "counterproductive."

"We are disappointed every day that there is not a decision to provide the Palestinian Authority these funds because we believe the decision to withhold them is counterproductive," he added at his daily briefing.

"Ambassador Ross did not indicate to me any particular feeling of being doublecrossed," he added. "But hopefully with a day or two, when we start to see some actions, this will become moot because Prime Minister Netanyahu himself has said that with actions will go easing of these measures."
He was referring to actions by Palestinian President Yasser Arafat, who is under U.S. and Israeli pressure to coordinate more closely with Israel on security.
"This whole process would be a lot easier if Chairman Arafat would understand the wisdom of making the security cooperation part and parcel of his policies," Rubin said.

Asked about a visit to Syria by Israeli Arabs including members of the Israeli parliament, the spokesman said he did not know of any progress they had made toward a resumption of talks between Israel and Syria.
"I am not aware that ... people are suddenly preparing their negotiating tables," he said.

He declined to take sides in the long-running dispute over whether talks should resume where they left off in early 1996, as Syria demands, or whether the Israeli government elected in mid-1996 has the right to change its negotiating position.
"Those are the two positions. That's fairly well known. Our position is to work to find ways, to find a formula to reconcile those two views," Rubin said.
